opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the questions we think about the most, because consistency is really where a world model either feels like a world or falls apart. With something like Genie, you're generating frames autoregressively, so every new frame is conditioned on what came before plus the action the user takes. Small errors can compound over time, and the classic failure mode is that you walk away from something, turn back around, and it's changed or disappeared.

So a lot of how we assess it is fairly direct. We look at whether the world stays coherent when you revisit places. If you move left and then move back right, is the environment still the same? Do objects persist? Does the layout hold together? Those revisitation tests are a pretty intuitive probe of whether the model has some kind of implicit memory of the scene rather than just generating plausible-looking frames moment to moment.

We also look at controllability over longer horizons. Early on, a model might respond correctly to actions for a few seconds, but you want to know if the actions still have consistent effects a minute in. If pressing "jump" always does roughly the same thing, that tells you the model has learned something meaningful about the latent action space and isn't drifting.

Then there's the visual quality side. Over long rollouts you can see degradation: blurriness, artifacts, the scene slowly melting. So we track how fidelity holds up as a function of time, and we use standard video metrics alongside a lot of qualitative inspection. Honestly, human judgment still matters a lot here, because metrics don't always capture whether something *feels* consistent or physically plausible.

And I'd say the honest answer is that it's still an open problem. We've seen real improvements in how long the model can maintain a coherent world, but pushing that horizon out further, so you can explore for minutes rather than seconds without things breaking down, is one of the main frontiers. It matters not just for interactive experiences, but especially if you want to use these environments to train agents, because an agent needs a world that behaves reliably to learn anything useful from it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so consistency is really one of the central questions for us with Genie, and it's something we think about in a few different ways. The first is just what I'd call visual or world consistency over long horizons. When you take an action, say you move the character to the left and then come back, does the thing that was there before still appear the way it did? And because Genie is generating each frame autoregressively, conditioned on the previous frames and the latent actions, there's always this potential for drift. Small errors can compound. So one of the ways we assess that is by having the model play out long trajectories and then looking at how stable the scene stays, whether objects persist, whether the physics of the world, like how a character jumps or falls, stays coherent across many steps.

The second piece is what we think of as action consistency, which is really specific to the latent action model. The whole idea in Genie is that we learn the action space in an unsupervised way from video, so there's no label telling us that a given latent code means "jump." What we want is for that latent action to mean the same thing across very different contexts. So if action three means move right in one environment, it should still mean move right when you're in a totally different scene, or even one generated from a sketch or a photograph. We evaluate that by applying the same sequence of latent actions across many different starting frames and checking whether the resulting motion is semantically consistent, and we also look at it through things like controllability metrics, where we measure how much the next frame actually depends on the action you took versus just being predicted from the past frames alone.

And then honestly, a lot of it is still qualitative. You sit down and play with it for a while and you notice the failure modes. Sometimes it holds together remarkably well, and sometimes the world kind of morphs on you after enough steps. Those long-horizon memory issues are, I think, one of the most important open problems for this whole class of models, and it's a big part of what we're pushing on going forward.

astra-6.text: I’d look at whether it preserves the state of the world as you keep interacting with it. If you move away from something and come back, is it still there? Do the same actions have consistent effects? A short clip can look convincing, but extended play gives you more opportunities to see things drift. So I’d distinguish visual consistency from whether the environment’s underlying behavior stays coherent. You really want to test both over longer sequences, rather than judge it from a few good examples.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate visual consistency from consistency in how the world behaves. As you play for longer, does the environment still look coherent, but also, do the same actions have the same effects? If you move away from a location and come back, does it preserve what was there? Those are different demands on the model.

The history here doesn’t give us results from extended play, so I wouldn’t claim that Genie maintains consistency over a particular duration. To assess that, I’d want longer rollouts that deliberately revisit places and repeat interactions, rather than judging it from a short, convincing clip.
